title: Browsers already block the leaked certificate keys. Your servers might not
dek: Eight certificate authority keys anyone can recover, and the fix that has to reach every container and runtime, not just Chrome. Also: TypeScript gets faster twice, curl opens its bug queue, and a game that ships its own bot army.

tldr.text: The private keys of **eight eMudhra intermediate certificates** can be recovered by anyone. Browsers blocked them; servers, containers and runtimes need their own updates, and Node.js and Bun were still pending.
TypeScript 7.1 beta type-checks up to **1.9x faster** than 7.0 on the team's test projects, and Cloudflare showed an experimental Rust port it says is up to 8x faster again.
curl will take low and medium security reports in public from October 26, to cope with a flood of AI-found reports. Two critical PHP fixes land today at 14:00 UTC.
About **36% of Steam Next Fest demos** now disclose generative AI, up from nearly 20% in June. GameDiscoverCo argues most studios should still keep their demos up.
A solo developer ran **37,800 bot playthroughs in 154 seconds** inside the shipping build of a new Steam game, and found six ways to print money.

blocks.title: Eight leaked certificate keys: patch more than your browser
blocks.gist: A certificate authority made eight of its signing keys so badly that anyone can work them out, letting an attacker fake a secure connection to any website. Browsers were patched fast; much other software was not.
blocks.background: eMudhra is an Indian certificate authority whose certificates chain up to roots trusted by Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Google.
blocks.takeaway: Your browser is fine. Your backend, your CI images and your command-line tools each carry their own list of trusted certificates, and each one needs updating and rebuilding.
body: On October 17 a researcher showed that the private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate certificates, created in April 2025, can be recovered from the certificates themselves. The proof was a message signed with every one of them. With such a key, anyone can issue a valid-looking certificate for any domain.

Firefox and Chrome blocked the certificates the same day, Apple on October 19 and Microsoft on October 20, and eMudhra has revoked them. No certificates from these intermediates appear in the public logs browsers require, so browsers were probably never exposed. Nobody knows whether attackers used the keys against other clients.

Those other clients are the problem. Servers, scripts, mobile apps and containers often check certificates against a bundle shipped with the operating system, the language runtime or a library, and many never check revocation. Each of those bundles has to be updated, and every container image rebuilt.

stat.label: intermediate certificates whose private keys anyone can recover

nodes.label: Browsers
nodes.note: blocked October 17 to 20 through their own revocation lists: nothing to do

nodes.label: Operating systems
nodes.note: fixed ca-certificates in Debian, Ubuntu, Alpine, Fedora, Homebrew: update

nodes.label: Language runtimes
nodes.note: Go, Python certifi, pip, uv, Rust webpki fixed; Node.js and Bun pending

nodes.label: Container images
nodes.note: keep the old bundle until you rebuild them

nodes.label: macOS system curl
nodes.note: no revocation check and an old bundle: needs a manual distrust

diagram.caption: Who still accepts a certificate forged with a recovered key depends on which trust bundle does the checking. Status as listed on the incident page on October 20.

blocks.why: Most production traffic between services never touches a browser. Until each runtime, base image and app bundle is updated, a forged certificate from these intermediates could pass as real there.
blocks.forYou: Rebuild the Docker images behind the SaaS backends and CI, and keep an eye on Node.js: it is the runtime the Supabase edge and Node services depend on, and its fix was still pending. Flutter apps that pin their own bundle need the same check.

terms.def: An organisation trusted to vouch that a website really is who it says, by signing its certificate.
Certificates a certificate authority uses for day-to-day signing, themselves signed by a more carefully guarded root.
The secret half of a key pair; whoever holds it can sign things that others will trust.
Marking a certificate as no longer valid before it expires, so clients that check will reject it.
The list of trusted root and intermediate certificates a program uses to decide which connections are genuine.

deep: Fixed versions listed by the incident page: Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10; Python certifi 2026.10.19, pip 26.2.2, uv 0.13.4; rustls-webpki 0.103.16 and webpki-roots 1.0.10; Electron 44.9.1, 43.8.1, 42.11.16; NSS 3.131.1; the curl CA bundle of 2026-10-20; Composer ca-bundle 1.4.16 and 1.6.0; Alpine ca-certificates 20261020-r0; Debian 20250419+deb13u1 and 20250419~deb12u2; Ubuntu 20260816ubuntu0.24.04.1 (and siblings); Homebrew ca-certificates 2026-09-25_1; cloudflared 2026.10.2. Pending: Node.js, Bun and FreeBSD ca_root_nss.

Test hosts: `https://dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/` and `https://dv-g3b-aaa-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/`. A certificate error means the client no longer trusts the compromised intermediates; a page that loads means it still does. The affected roots are Comodo AAA Services and emSign ECC Root CA - G3.

Cloudflare's advice: update the HTTP library, runtime and OS trust store underneath your SDK, not just the SDK; rebuild images and restart services; never fix new certificate errors by turning verification off; and test through the application's real connection path, because a passing browser or curl test does not prove a background service is protected.

blocks.title: curl moves minor security reports into the open
blocks.gist: The team behind curl, a networking tool inside billions of devices, is drowning in security reports, many found by AI. From October 26 it will handle the less serious ones in public instead of in private.
blocks.speaker: Daniel Stenberg
blocks.context: From October 26, reports rated low or medium go to public GitHub issues; only high and critical stay private. Stenberg says over 90% of recent reports could quickly be rated below high.
blocks.why: Open source projects are rewriting their security process around a flood of AI-generated reports. Expect a faster, noisier stream of curl advisories in the base images you ship.
blocks.forYou: If you ever publish a security policy for the plugins, this is a template: keep only the serious tier private.

blocks.title: GitHub puts a firewall between your agents and npm
blocks.gist: GitHub is testing a filter that sits between the machines that install packages (build servers, coding agents) and the npm registry, and blocks downloads that look malicious or are too new to trust.
blocks.intro: Install-time malware steals credentials the moment a package is installed, and agents install packages unattended. The firewall checks every request on the way through.

nodes.label: Package firewall
nodes.note: policy set by the organisation's admins

nodes.label: Checks
nodes.note: cooldown for new versions, Advisory Database, attestation downgrades

nodes.label: npm registry
nodes.note: the only registry supported in the preview

blocks.caption: The flow described in GitHub's changelog. Blocked packages can be released through an exception request.
blocks.why: A cooldown on brand-new package versions is the cheapest defence against the poisoned-update attacks that keep hitting npm, and it matters more when an agent runs the install.
blocks.forYou: This is Enterprise Cloud only, so not directly usable on a personal account; the cooldown idea is the part to copy into your own install habits for agent sessions.

terms.def: The main package registry and installer for JavaScript and TypeScript code.
A waiting period during which newly published package versions are not installed, giving time for malware to be spotted.
A package version that suddenly arrives without the signed build proof its earlier versions had, a sign of tampering.

deep: Public preview for all GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data residency; free during the preview, metered billing like Actions at general availability. Endpoints have to be configured to route package requests through the firewall.

blocks.title: Supabase hands your coding agent a read-only view of production
blocks.gist: Supabase published ready-made prompts and tools that let a coding agent check a live project's health, security and speed on a schedule, without being able to change anything.
blocks.intro: Connect Supabase's MCP server to one project in read-only mode, then install the updated agent skill:
blocks.code:
claude mcp add --scope project --transport http supabase "https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp?project_ref=abc123&read_only=true"
npx skills add supabase/agent-skills
explain: Replace `abc123` with your project ref, then authenticate under `/mcp`. With `read_only=true` every query runs as a read-only Postgres user, and a new `query_logs` tool reads up to 24 hours of logs per call.

Four prompts come with suggested schedules: health and performance hourly, security and resource growth daily. Scheduled runs cannot stop for approval, so pre-approve only the read-only tools, and run each prompt once by hand first.
blocks.why: It is a ready-made pattern for letting an agent watch production: read-only credentials, narrow prompts, and reports that list only new problems.
blocks.forYou: This drops straight into a routine for the Supabase-backed SaaS products: start with the daily security prompt on one project.

terms.def: Model Context Protocol: a standard way to give an AI agent tools, such as querying a database.
The open-source database Supabase is built on.

deep: Also shipped: a Health tab in Advisors and a Database Connections page in the dashboard (on for every project, including self-hosted; it can cancel queries, so it is not read-only). The prompts tell the agent to ignore instructions found inside logs or query results. To report only new or worsening findings, the agent tool has to keep alert state between runs. For small projects Supabase suggests one prompt on a daily or weekly schedule.

sources.label: Supabase: check production with your coding agent

blocks.title: TypeScript 7.1 beta checks big projects up to twice as fast
blocks.gist: The TypeScript team's next version finds type errors faster than the one released this summer, with the biggest gains on the largest projects in its tests.
blocks.intro: Speedup over TypeScript 7.0 when checking types only, with four checker threads, as measured by the TypeScript team.
blocks.note: Vendor-reported. mui-docs went from 22.2 s to 11.9 s; memory use fell 16% to 50% across the five projects.
blocks.why: Type checking is the cheapest test a coding agent can run on its own changes. Faster checks mean tighter agent loops and shorter CI runs.
blocks.forYou: Try the beta on one of the React or Node repos and time `tsc --noEmit` before and after; read the breaking changes first.

terms.def: Mistakes such as passing text where a number is expected, which TypeScript catches before the code runs.

deep: Install with `npm install -D typescript@beta`. New: `--target es2026` is stable, `import source` declarations, `Promise.allKeyed`, `Iterator.zip` and `Iterator.prototype.chunks` under `--lib esnext`, new `typescript/sync`, `typescript/fs` and `typescript/ast` API entry points, and content mappers for Vue, Svelte and MDX. Breaking: a regenerated DOM lib.d.ts and stricter checks on distributive type parameters.

blocks.title: Claude Code 2.1.305 and 2.1.306: the changes worth knowing
blocks.gist: Two Claude Code updates fix a bug that broke every request behind some company gateways, stop resumed workflows redoing finished work, and quietly change which managed MCP servers load.
blocks.intro: Version 2.1.305 is a large release; 2.1.306 followed with two fixes. Update to 2.1.306.

items.title: Gateway regression fixed
items.text: On 2.1.304, every request could fail on Vertex, Bedrock or a gateway that rejects tool search. It now retries without it.

items.title: Workflow resume skips finished agents
items.text: Resuming a workflow no longer re-runs agents that already completed inside `pipeline()` or `parallel()`; their results come from the run's journal.

items.title: Managed MCP servers may now load
items.text: `allowedMcpServers` stops filtering `managed-mcp.json` stdio servers that use `${VAR}` only in `env`. Use `deniedMcpServers` to keep one off.

items.title: Sandbox can allow nested namespaces
items.text: `sandbox.allowNestedUserNamespaces` lets sandboxed Linux commands such as Chromium run, at the cost of weaker file protection.

items.title: Unattended retries notice a lifted limit
items.text: `CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_USAGE_LIMIT_RECHECK_MS` sets how often retry mode rechecks a usage limit before its reset time.

items.title: Real errors in big MCP sessions
items.text: 2.1.306 stops a real API error showing up as "prompt is too long" and forcing a compaction in sessions with many MCP tools.

blocks.why: If you run Claude Code through a cloud provider or a company gateway, 2.1.304 could stop it working; and the MCP allowlist change can load a server you meant to keep off.
blocks.forYou: Check managed-mcp.json after updating, and the Chromium sandbox setting is what Playwright tests for the three.js games need inside the sandbox.

terms.def: A proxy a company puts between its staff and an AI provider to control access and costs.
When an agent summarises its earlier conversation to free up room in its context.

blocks.title: Should you pull your demo because of AI cloners? Usually not
blocks.gist: After two well-wishlisted games pulled public demos over fears of AI-assisted cloning, the games market analyst GameDiscoverCo set out when that fear is justified and when it is not.
blocks.plain: Clone risk depends on how easy your idea is to copy and how easily players can search for it, not on whether a demo exists.
body: Drunken Goddess Reflux, with an estimated 570,000 wishlists, cancelled its public demo, and ReVamp, with about 250,000, swapped its Steam playtest for a closed one. GameDiscoverCo's view: most clones are made by hand, are not popular and do not scale, so they are not worth losing a demo over.
points: Complex game, some momentum, distinctive name: keep the demo and playtests.
Simple, casual, meme-able idea with a searchable name: shorten the gap from reveal to launch instead.
If a decompiled copy of your code takes off, document it and report it to Steam as copyright infringement.
blocks.why: Demos remain one of the strongest wishlist drivers on Steam. Pulling one out of fear costs real players for a risk that mostly hits simple, copyable ideas.
blocks.forYou: Plugin-based action RPGs are hard to clone from a demo; the risk applies more to a small, searchable browser game concept.

terms.def: Players saving a game on Steam to be told when it launches; the main early sign of demand.
Turned from a shipped program back into readable source code.

deep: GameDiscoverCo cites the needle-in-a-haystack micro-genre as the clone case: a simple concept shown in videos in late August, with no playable version, was copied quickly because the idea was simple and the name searchable. The same post notes Next Fest had about 7,100 playable demos against about 5,000 predicted by the trend line.

blocks.title: 37,800 bot runs in 154 seconds, inside the shipping game
blocks.gist: A solo developer built a balance-testing harness into the actual build of a new Steam trading game: bots of three skill levels play thousands of seeded runs, and the numbers show which loops break the economy.
blocks.intro: O'BLOCK, a free sneaker-flipping game, launched on Steam on October 20. Its developer says Claude Code wrote most of its 40,000 lines, while they designed the game, set the rules and decided what was fun.

steps.title: Put the harness in the real build
steps.text: One environment variable skips the window, plays headless bot runs and writes a report, so the tests run against exactly what players get.

steps.title: Write three kinds of player
steps.text: A random button-masher, a sensible player who reads prices, and an exploit seeker that hunts for loops. All see only what a human sees and obey the same limits.

steps.title: Run many seeds per mode
steps.text: 300 seeds per cell across four modes: 37,800 full runs in 154 seconds on two threads, each replayable from its seed.

steps.title: Check invariants
steps.text: No negative cash, no NaN money, no empty stacks. The run found zero violations.

steps.title: Compare the bots
steps.text: In the open-ended mode the seeker's 90th percentile net worth was about 16 times the sensible player's, which pointed to six money printers, such as same-day buy and resell.

blocks.why: Agents now write game code fast enough that balance and economy bugs pile up faster than people can playtest. Bots that play the real build turn balance into a number you can track.
blocks.forYou: The inventory and combat plugins could ship a headless harness like this as a feature: a simulated player per policy, run in CI, with a per-bot table in the report.

terms.def: Running a program without a window or screen, so it can run fast on a server.
Starting numbers for the random generator; the same seed replays the same game exactly.
Rules that must always be true in a program, such as cash never going below zero.
The value that 90% of results fall below; a way to look at the best runs without the single luckiest one.

deep: Bots are a `Policy` enum in the game's Rust code: Random, Reader and Seeker. In the billion-dollar mode, Random was evicted every time, Reader won 81% (median day 43) and Seeker won only 7%. In the 90-day tycoon mode, p90 net worth was $21.48B for Random, $914.62B for Reader and $14,460.33B for Seeker. Exploits measured per dollar in: top-rung mark multiplier 27.1x, stacked angles 12x, lot slicing 6.55x, connects 6.34x, relisted outlet pallets 2.49x, and same-day resale returning 1,763.8% across 9,812 sales. Seeker runs past the sane bound fell from 493 of 4,200 on October 6 to 73 after four passes of fixes; the launch build measured 82.
The developer also notes an AI-written report that listed three exploits as live after the CSV showed them fixed: check generated summaries against the raw data.

learn.question: What is a chain of trust, and why can one bad link break it?
learn.answer: When your app connects securely to a server, the server shows a certificate, signed by an intermediate, signed in turn by a root your system already trusts. Your app accepts the server only if every signature in that chain checks out.
learn.analogy: Like a passport: a border officer trusts it because a government issued it, and trusts the government's stamp because it is on a short list they already hold. Steal the stamp and you can print passports anyone will accept.
body: Roots are kept offline and used rarely, so certificate authorities do daily signing with intermediates. That makes an intermediate's private key as powerful as the root for anyone who gets it: they can sign a certificate for any domain, and clients will follow the chain up to a root they trust.

Two things limit the damage. Revocation lets clients learn that a certificate should no longer be trusted, and certificate transparency logs make every issued certificate public, so browsers that require a log entry refuse certificates nobody has seen. Many non-browser clients do neither, which is why today's leaked keys need fixes in every trust bundle.

nodes.label: Root certificate
nodes.note: pre-installed in your OS, browser or runtime; signs intermediates

nodes.label: Intermediate certificate
nodes.note: does the daily signing; today's leaked keys are here

nodes.label: Server certificate
nodes.note: names one domain, signed by the intermediate

nodes.label: Your client
nodes.note: follows the signatures up to a root it trusts

diagram.caption: Each layer vouches for the one below. A client trusts the server only if every signature leads to a root in its own trust bundle.

terms.def: A top-level certificate that operating systems and browsers ship with and trust without question.
Public, append-only logs of every certificate issued, so misissued ones can be spotted.

tryThis.title: Give your game three bots and let them play overnight
tryThis.gist: A small headless harness with a random, a sensible and an exploit-hunting player turns game balance into a table of numbers you can compare after every change.
tryThis.needs: A game or gameplay system whose rules can run without rendering, such as an economy, a crafting loop or a combat simulation.

steps.title: Add a headless switch
steps.text: Behind an environment variable or command-line flag, skip the window and run the game loop as fast as it will go, writing results to a file.

steps.title: Write three policies
steps.text: Random picks any legal action. Sensible follows the obvious good play. Seeker repeats whichever action gained the most last time. Give them only what a player can see.

steps.title: Seed every run
steps.text: Run a few hundred seeds per bot and record the seed with each result, so any odd run can be replayed exactly.

steps.title: Assert your invariants
steps.text: After every step, check the rules that must hold: no negative money, no impossible counts. Fail the run with its seed when one breaks.

steps.title: Print a per-bot table
steps.text: Median and 90th percentile of your main score for each bot. Put it in CI, so a balance change shows up as a number in the build log.

tryThis.check: Random loses, sensible wins most runs, and the seeker does not beat the sensible player by a wide margin. If it does, replay its best seed to see which loop it found.

terms.def: The rules a bot uses to choose its next move.

tryThis.forYou: Start with the inventory plugin's crafting and trading loop as a commandlet that runs headless in the editor build.

sparks.title: People are using coding agents to strip ads from their TVs
sparks.signal: A few thousand people modified their TVs within two days of one project's post, TechCrunch reports.
sparks.hook: Point Claude Code at a TV over the network and ask it to remove bloatware and swap the launcher; one user cut a 192 MB launcher to 83 MB.
sparks.borrow: A repo of instructions that an agent follows on the user's own device is a new way to ship a tool. It also bricked at least one TV, so build in a way back.
sparks.forYou: The instructions-for-an-agent repo is a distribution idea for plugin setup scripts.

lab.title: TraceLite: Efficient Trace Reduction for SWE Agents via Optical Compression and Redundancy Removal
lab.headline: Squeeze a coding agent's old tool output, and it uses a third fewer tokens with no loss of success.
lab.authors: Jingyu Xiao, Qianxi Liu, Yintong Huo et al. (Chinese University of Hong Kong, Dalian University of Technology, Singapore Management University)
lab.problem: A coding agent's context grows with every command it runs, and most of the old output is stale or repeated, which costs money and attention.
lab.idea: Keep the three newest observations as text, render older ones as images at four times compression, strip lines repeated between observations, and clear old file dumps after an edit. No training and no extra model calls.
lab.result: On 400 SWE-bench Verified tasks it solved 78.25% against 78.00% with the full trace, with 33% fewer input tokens. It beat AgentDiet, SWE-Pruner and LLMLingua2 on solve rate; LongCodeZip cut more tokens but solved 13.75 points fewer.
lab.useIt: The cheap half works without vision: dedupe repeated lines in tool output and drop stale pre-edit file contents, then compare tokens per task on a few of your usual jobs.
lab.forYou: A PostToolUse hook that trims repeated test and build output is the experiment to try.

image.alt: TraceLite overview: an agent loop; older observations turned into compact images while recent ones stay as text; overlapping lines removed and history cleared after an edit.

lab.title: Documentation Drift in AI-Generated Pull Requests
lab.headline: Nearly two thirds of coding-agent pull requests change code without touching any documentation.
lab.authors: Will De Michele, Kla Tantithamthavorn (Monash University)
lab.problem: Agents now open many pull requests on public repositories. Nobody had measured whether they keep the docs in step with the code.
lab.idea: Check 29,669 agent pull requests from 2,585 repositories for whether code changes came with a documentation change, by agent and by kind of task, and follow the files for 90 days.
lab.result: 63.2% changed code with no doc update: 55.2% of feature work and 77.5% of refactors. Claude Code had the lowest rate at 48.1%, Devin the highest at 72.8%. Files changed without docs were re-documented within 90 days 24% of the time, against 48% for documented ones.
lab.useIt: Add a check to your agent's review step that flags code changes with no matching README, docs or changelog edit when behaviour changes.
lab.forYou: Plugin buyers read the docs; a doc co-change check in the plugin repos' review skill is cheap.

links.label: arXiv: Documentation Drift in AI-Generated PRs

image.alt: Bar chart of documentation co-change rate by pull request type: feat 44.8%, chore 43.9%, docs 43.2% down to ci 12.7% and style 11.2%; overall 36.8%.

lab.title: RCPG: Real-Time Product Path Guiding Using Radiance Cascades
lab.headline: Reusing radiance cascades lets a real-time path tracer aim its rays better, for about twice as many paths per pixel.
lab.authors: Julius Ikkala, Pekka Jääskeläinen, Markku Mäkitalo (Tampere University)
lab.problem: Real-time path tracers have to guess where light comes from. Guiding usually samples incoming light and surface reflection separately and blends them, wasting samples.
lab.idea: Bound the radiance stored in radiance cascades so they keep accurate light directions, then sample the product of light and surface reflection in one step. The world-space structure also guides bounces that start off screen.
lab.result: The authors report generally about twice as many paths per pixel at real-time rates compared with earlier real-time guiding that combines several samplers. It works alongside unbiased ReSTIR.
lab.useIt: A reference for anyone building a custom path-traced or global illumination pass; radiance cascades are already popular for 2D lighting.
lab.forYou: Background for judging Lumen alternatives; no code to drop in.

image.alt: Diagram of two cascade levels: incoming radiance times the surface reflection term gives a product grid; the chosen cell in cascade 0 leads to a finer cell in cascade 1.
image.credit: Ikkala, Jääskeläinen and Mäkitalo, Tampere University
